questions.question_text: In the context of the Node.js File System module, what is the primary operational difference between fs.writeFileSync and fs.appendFileSync when interacting with an existing file?
questions.option_a: fs.writeFileSync is asynchronous, while fs.appendFileSync is synchronous.
questions.option_b: fs.writeFileSync overwrites the existing content of the file, whereas fs.appendFileSync adds new content to the end without modifying previous data.
questions.option_c: fs.writeFileSync creates a new file only if it does not exist, while fs.appendFileSync creates a new file if it does not exist.
questions.option_d: fs.writeFileSync is restricted to text files, while fs.appendFileSync can handle binary data only.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because the lecture explicitly distinguishes these two methods: fs.writeFileSync overwrites the file's content, while fs.appendFileSync preserves existing content and adds new data to the end. Option A is incorrect because both methods are synchronous (indicated by the 'Sync' suffix). Option C is incorrect because both methods will create the file if it does not exist, but their behavior regarding existing content differs. Option D is incorrect because both methods can handle various data types, not just text or binary exclusively.
questions.what_taught: The distinction between overwriting (writeFileSync) and appending (appendFileSync) file operations.
questions.why_assessed: To ensure students understand the side effects of different file writing methods to prevent accidental data loss.
evidence_refs: Factual_Summary: writing to files with fs.writeFileSync (which overwrites existing content)
questions.misconception_rationale: Distractors target common confusions about sync/async nature and file creation behavior.

questions.question_text: A developer needs to remove a directory named 'logs' from the file system. Which Node.js File System method should they use?
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because fs.rmdirSync is the specific method for removing directories, analogous to the Linux 'rmdir' command. Option A is incorrect because fs.unlinkSync is restricted to deleting files and cannot be used for directories. Option C is incorrect because writing an empty string to a directory path is not a valid removal operation and may cause an error. Option D is incorrect because fs.mkdirSync is used to create directories, not remove them.
questions.what_taught: The specific use of fs.rmdirSync for directory deletion versus file deletion.
questions.why_assessed: To verify students can select the correct API for directory management tasks.
evidence_refs: Factual_Summary: fs.rmdirSync is required for directory removal
questions.misconception_rationale: Distractors include the file deletion method (unlinkSync) which is a common error when students conflate file and directory operations.

questions.question_text: What is the primary security purpose of using 'Safe Buffers' in memory allocation?
questions.option_a: To increase the speed of data retrieval by pre-allocating large memory blocks.
questions.option_b: To ensure that allocated memory space is initialized to zeros, preventing information leakage from previous memory contents.
questions.option_c: To allow the buffer to automatically resize when more data is written than the allocated space.
questions.option_d: To encrypt the data stored in the buffer before it is written to the file system.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because the lecture defines Safe Buffers as memory allocations initialized to zeros to prevent residual data from previous operations from being exposed. Option A is incorrect because safe buffers are about security, not speed optimization. Option C is incorrect because buffers have a fixed size and do not automatically resize. Option D is incorrect because safe buffers do not perform encryption; they only initialize memory to zero.
questions.what_taught: The definition and security benefit of zero-initialized memory buffers.
questions.why_assessed: To assess understanding of low-level memory security concepts relevant to handling sensitive data.
evidence_refs: Factual_Summary: safe buffers, where memory is initialized to zeros
questions.misconception_rationale: Distractors reflect misconceptions about buffer functionality (resizing, encryption) and performance vs. security trade-offs.

questions.question_text: In a 60-byte buffer, if a name is written at index 0 and an email is written at index 20, what characterizes the memory space between the end of the name and the start of the email?
questions.option_a: It contains random garbage data from previous operations.
questions.option_b: It is filled with null characters (zero bytes) because the buffer was initialized to zeros.
questions.option_c: It is compressed to save memory space.
questions.option_d: It is automatically filled with the last character of the name to maintain continuity.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because the lecture explains that buffers are allocated with zero-initialized memory (safe buffers), so any space not explicitly written to remains as zero bytes. Option A is incorrect because safe buffers prevent garbage data from previous operations. Option C is incorrect because buffers do not compress data. Option D is incorrect because there is no automatic filling mechanism; the space remains zero.
questions.what_taught: How data placement in a buffer affects the state of unused memory segments.
questions.why_assessed: To test the ability to visualize and analyze memory layout based on buffer initialization rules.
evidence_refs: Factual_Summary: resulting in a gap of zero bytes between the two fields
questions.misconception_rationale: Distractors target misconceptions about uninitialized memory (garbage data) and automatic data manipulation (compression/filling).

questions.question_text: When reading from a buffer, what is the effect of specifying only a starting index without an ending index?
questions.option_a: It reads only the single byte at the starting index.
questions.option_b: It reads from the starting index to the end of the buffer.
questions.option_c: It returns an error because both start and end indices are required.
questions.option_d: It reads from the beginning of the buffer to the starting index.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because the lecture states that providing just a start index allows the system to read to the end of the buffer. Option A is incorrect because it reads a range, not a single byte. Option C is incorrect because the end index is optional. Option D is incorrect because the range is from the start index forward, not backward.
questions.what_taught: The syntax and behavior of extracting substrings from buffers using start/end indices.
questions.why_assessed: To ensure students understand the default behavior of buffer reading functions when parameters are omitted.
questions.misconception_rationale: Distractors reflect errors in understanding index directionality and parameter requirements.
